title: Desire as a god
hook: have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god (45:23)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the smoke, and your line was a sign in the sky. Did you look up, and remember a relief you forgot to give thanks for? Day five hundred seventy-four, the end of the week.

It's eleven at night. You said you'd sleep early. One more episode. Then one more scroll. Then the fridge, for nothing in particular. Nobody forced any of it. Nobody would call it worship, either. It's just wanting, doing what wanting does when nobody stops it. But Surah Al-Jathiyah, the Kneeling, the forty-fifth surah, uses exactly that word. It asks about a person whose wanting has quietly taken the top place in their life, the place the Qur'an keeps for God alone.

Pickthall's translation of verse twenty-three begins: "Hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god." The Arabic word for desire is hawa. The dictionaries tie its root to falling, or being blown, the way something drops through the air with nothing under it. Hawa is wanting that pulls you along without asking where it's going. The verse doesn't say desire is evil. Muslim teaching makes room for appetite: food, marriage, rest, beauty, each in its place. The problem the verse names is rank. When the wanting decides and everything else obeys, the wanting has become a god, even if the person never bowed to an idol in their life. The rest of the verse is sobering: it speaks of hearing and heart sealed, and a covering on the sight. Many commentators read that as what slowly happens when every choice runs one way. Classical writers turned this into a whole teaching. Al-Ghazali wrote at length about the struggle with the nafs, the self that wants, and used the picture of a mount and its rider: strong, useful, and safe only when the rider holds the reins. Another verse in the Qur'an, in Surah An-Nazi'at, praises the one who feared standing before his Lord and held the self back from hawa. So the word is not a word for sin. It's a word for direction. Is the mount carrying you, or are you being carried off? This week has moved through consultation, daughters and sons, silver roofs, friends that last, a blessed night and a smoke in the sky. It ends on a plain question: who, or what, sits on the throne inside you.
screen: `HAWA: DESIRE THAT PULLS YOU ALONG.` · `NOT EVIL, BUT OUT OF RANK.` · `THE SELF AS A MOUNT NEEDING A RIDER.` · `WHO SITS ON THE THRONE INSIDE?`

segments.voice: The practice: refuse one craving. Sit, and breathe. Let one small craving come up: a snack, your phone, a purchase, a reply you want to send too fast. Don't fight it. Just watch it, the way you'd watch weather. Notice where it lives in the body. Then decide, quietly, that this one will wait until tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask for help holding it. The bell holds the time.
Hawa. Desire that pulls you along, the wanting that 45:23 warns can take a god's place when nothing else is allowed to rank above it. Today's word.
Your line: not my desire's servant. Today, the first time you reach for something out of pure habit, pause for three seconds and ask who's deciding. Day five hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs and its hawa; many practice small refusals through voluntary fasts on Mondays and Thursdays, and classical spiritual writing treats taming desire as daily work.

fork.setup: you notice a craving at eleven at night. what does 45:23 ask you to look at?
options: who or what is ranking first in your choices.
fork.reveal: the verse is about rank: desire made a god, deciding while everything else obeys.

original.note: Arabic: desire, inclination; the root carries a sense of falling or being blown.

trapdoor: what you thought: wanting things is the problem.
what it means: desire becomes a god when it takes the top place and everything else obeys it.
what a scholar hears: hawa shares a root with falling through the air; 79:40 praises the one who held the self back from hawa.
